title: Three‐Phase Mobilization of Organic Phosphorus Sustains Phosphorus Bioavailability Under Long‐Term Nitrogen Addition in a Subtropical Plantation
content:
Three-phased phosphorus (P) supply model illustrates that the primary source of soil bioavailable P under nitrogen (N) addition shifts over the course of the experiment. To satisfy the increasing demand for plant P, soil bioavailable P is initially derived from labile organic P. Over time, it shifts to moderately labile organic P and eventually to stable organic P. The progressive mobilization of organic P is coupled with increased plant belowground carbon investment, enhanced microbially mediated production of organic acids and phosphatases, soil acidification, and declining soil P sorption capacity. The “+” and “−” symbols indicate overall significant increases and decreases of the respective indicators within each N addition phase, respectively. The number of symbols denotes the relative magnitude of change, facilitating visual comparisons across different phases.


ABSTRACT

Nitrogen (N) input is expected to intensify phosphorus (P) limitation in tropical and subtropical forests. However, how soil and microbial processes mobilize P from poorly available pools to sustain soil P bioavailability remains unclear. We conducted a nine-year experiment with low (20 kg N ha−1 year−1) and high (80 kg N ha−1 year−1) N addition treatments in a subtropical Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) plantation. We quantified soil P fractions, P-cycling functional genes, phosphatase activity, P sorption capacity (PSC), iron and aluminum oxides, and plant properties throughout the experiment. Our results reveal three distinct stages in the regulation of soil bioavailable P with prolonged N addition. Phase I: N addition reduces P bioavailability, and labile organic P decomposition becomes the main source of bioavailable P, associated with increased phosphatase activity. Phase II: when labile organic P becomes insufficient to meet P demand, bioavailable P is replenished through the depletion of moderately labile organic P; this is related to decreased PSC and enhanced acid phosphomonoesterases activity. Phase III: stable organic P decreases significantly, jointly sustaining bioavailable P with the depletion of other organic P fractions, alongside a further decrease in PSC and enriched microbial organic acid- and phosphatase-related genes. This study uncovers a novel “three-phased P supply” model revealed through long-term observations. These mechanistic insights reveal the pathways of soil P mobilization under continuous N input in a subtropical forest and establish a framework for predicting the buffering capacity of soil P pools in P-limited ecosystems under global change scenarios.
